title: Private Deployments — Optimization Config Version Pinning + Rollback (Operator Guide, DRAFT)
content:
Audience
- Private deployment operators (SRE / platform team) running Redwood Inference in customer-managed environments.
- This doc assumes you can run helm upgrades and/or use the Redwood Private Installer CLI and that you have access to the Private control plane API endpoint.

What this guide covers (Private)
- Pin an Optimization Config version (batching/caching/quantization profiles) for a given scope.
- Safely roll forward during upgrades (runtime/control plane/chart versions) without accidentally changing optimization behavior.
- Execute a rollback to a known-good Optimization Config version with minimal downtime.

What this guide does NOT cover
- Designing gating metrics/thresholds (see SRE gate rules + rollout health dashboard spec).
- Fully automated rollback (no human confirmation) except where explicitly noted for internal environments.

Terms
- Optimization Config Version (OCV): immutable versioned config object stored in the control plane.
- Active version pointer: the version currently selected for a scope (tenant/model/region/etc.).
- Pinned: explicitly selecting a specific OCV and preventing automatic promotion.
- Scope: where the config applies. In Private, scope is typically at least {deployment, model} and optionally {region/cluster} depending on customer topology.

High-level model (Private)
1) The Private control plane stores Optimization Config Versions (immutable). Operators can create/import versions and set the active version pointer.
2) The serving runtime fetches the active version and applies it using an idempotent applier. Rollbacks are implemented as switching the active pointer back to a prior version (plus worker reconciliation).
3) In Private, the operator is responsible for:
   - Access control (RBAC) in their environment
   - Change windows and operational monitoring
   - Ensuring the runtime/control plane versions you deploy support the same versioning semantics

Prerequisites / before you touch prod
- Confirm platform versions
  - Control plane build includes Optimization Config Service + rollback endpoint.
  - Runtime build includes idempotent apply pipeline (race-safe).
  - Helm chart / installer supports version pinning values.
- Monitoring + observability
  - You should be able to observe (at minimum): 5xx rate, p95 latency, throughput, GPU utilization, and worker apply status.
  - Recommended: enable response header surfacing of active config version for debugging (if supported by your deployment).
- Permissions
  - Your operator identity must have the “optimization change operator” permissions for: list versions, set active version, rollback.
  - If you can’t see rollback actions in tooling or you get 403s, treat as an RBAC issue first (common).

Section A — Determine current active Optimization Config Version
Option 1: API (recommended)
- From a bastion / inside-cluster context, query the Private control plane.
- Example (illustrative; endpoints may differ by deployment):
  - GET /v1/optimization-configs/active?scope=deployment:prod&model=rw-llama-70b&region=us-east
  - Response should include: active_version_id, updated_at, updated_by

Option 2: Runtime response headers (debug)
- If enabled, check an inference response for the active version ID.
- Example headers:
  - x-redwood-optimization-config-version: ocv_2026_02_04_0012
  - x-redwood-model-version: rw-llama-70b@2026-01-30
- Notes:
  - Header surfacing is optional and may be disabled for some customer environments.
  - Do not depend on this for automation; it’s primarily for incident/debug workflows.

Option 3: Worker status command
- If you run the Private Installer CLI or have a runtime admin endpoint, validate workers are converged:
  - desired_version_id == applied_version_id across all worker pools

Section B — Pinning an Optimization Config Version
When to pin
- During sensitive periods (launches, month-end, major customer events) to prevent accidental config drift.
- Before/after platform upgrades when you want to keep optimization behavior stable.
- When running experiments: pin the baseline and pin the canary separately.

B1) Pinning via Helm (common path)
- In your values.yaml (example keys; confirm actual chart values in your chart version):

  optimizationConfig:
    mode: pinned
    versionId: ocv_2026_02_04_0012
    scope:
      deployment: prod
      model: rw-llama-70b
      region: us-east

- Apply with a standard helm upgrade:
  - helm upgrade redwood-private redwood/redwood-private -f values.yaml --namespace redwood

- Important
  - Pinning affects selection (active pointer) but workers still need to reconcile. Ensure you have a rolling strategy set (see Section D).

B2) Pinning via Private Installer CLI
- Example (illustrative):
  - redwood-private optimization-config pin \
      --deployment prod \
      --model rw-llama-70b \
      --region us-east \
      --version ocv_2026_02_04_0012 \
      --reason "Pin during control plane upgrade window"

- Expected behavior
  - CLI updates the active version pointer in the control plane and emits an audit event.

B3) Pinning via Terraform (for GitOps-style Private)
- If you use the Redwood Terraform provider, manage pins declaratively.
- Example (conceptual; confirm resource names):
  - resource "redwood_optimization_config_active" "prod_rw_llama_70b_us_east" {
      scope = "deployment:prod/model:rw-llama-70b/region:us-east"
      version_id = "ocv_2026_02_04_0012"
      pinned = true
    }

- Operational note
  - If you also allow in-console/manual changes, decide which is source-of-truth. Mixed workflows cause “flapping” pointers.

Section C — Handling upgrades without changing optimization behavior
Goal: upgrade runtime/control plane/chart versions while keeping Optimization Config stable.

Recommended upgrade approach
1) Record current active OCV
   - Save active_version_id + scope and a link to your change request.
2) Pin the OCV before the upgrade
   - Set mode=pinned to the current active version.
3) Upgrade control plane first
   - Run migrations / chart upgrade for control plane.
   - Validate Optimization Config Service health:
     - list versions
     - get active version
4) Upgrade runtime next (rolling)
   - Ensure runtime can read and apply the pinned version.
5) Post-upgrade validation
   - Confirm active pointer unchanged.
   - Confirm convergence: all workers applied_version_id == pinned version.
   - Confirm metrics within expected ranges.
6) Optional: unpin
   - Only after you’ve confirmed the new stack is stable and you want to allow future promotions.

Compatibility pitfalls during upgrades
- Schema evolution: newer control plane validators may reject older config shapes.
  - Mitigation: validate the pinned version using the new validator before upgrading runtime pools.
- Quantization profile compatibility: newer runtime may change supported quant modes.
  - Mitigation: have a known-good “unquantized or safe quant” fallback version ready.

Section D — Rollback procedure (minimal downtime)
Primary objective: revert optimization behavior quickly without causing a full serving outage.

When to rollback
- Sudden increase in 5xx.
- p95/p99 latency regression correlated with config change.
- Quality regression (for quantization changes) confirmed by eval harness or customer reports.
- Mis-scope (wrong region/model impacted).

Before you press rollback
- Identify blast radius
  - Which scopes are impacted? (deployment/model/region)
  - Is it partial rollout? If yes, do you rollback only canary scope or entire scope?
- Pick the target version
  - Prefer the last known-good version from your change record.
  - If unsure, rollback to the version immediately prior to the change.
- Confirm you’re not racing an in-progress apply
  - If your tooling shows an apply in progress, pause/stop the rollout controller first (if enabled) before switching the active pointer.

D1) Rollback using control plane API / console action
- Set active version pointer back to the target known-good version.
- Example (illustrative):
  - POST /v1/optimization-configs/rollback
    payload: scope, target_version_id, reason
- Expect
  - Audit event emitted (rollback requested)
  - Active pointer changes immediately
  - Workers reconcile shortly after (seconds to minutes depending on fleet size)

D2) Rollback using Helm (if you manage pointer via chart values)
- Update values.yaml:
  optimizationConfig:
    mode: pinned
    versionId: ocv_2026_01_28_0009   # last known-good

- Apply:
  - helm upgrade redwood-private redwood/redwood-private -f values.yaml --namespace redwood

- Notes
  - This is typically slower than a direct API rollback (depends on your CD pipeline), but it keeps GitOps consistency.

D3) Runtime reconciliation strategy (to minimize downtime)
- Use rolling restarts only if required
  - Many changes can be applied live via the idempotent applier.
  - If your runtime requires a restart for certain toggles (rare; depends on build), do a rolling restart with maxUnavailable=0.
- Recommended Kubernetes settings
  - PodDisruptionBudget: ensure at least N pods remain available.
  - RollingUpdate: maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 (tune for your cluster capacity).
  - Graceful draining: ensure pods stop receiving new requests before shutdown.

D4) Verify rollback success
- Convergence
  - desired_version_id == target_version_id
  - applied_version_id == target_version_id on all worker pools
  - No mixed states (a common symptom of apply/rollback races; this should be addressed in newer builds, but verify anyway)
- Metrics
  - 5xx returns to baseline
  - p95/p99 latency returns to baseline
  - Throughput stabilizes; GPU utilization returns to expected
- Quality (quantization)
  - Run a small, fast eval set if available (sanity checks) before declaring “resolved.”

Section E — Common pitfalls (Private)
1) Rollback “succeeds” but latency doesn’t recover
- Causes
  - You rolled back the wrong scope (e.g., only us-east but issue is global)
  - Cache invalidation / warmup effects after config change
  - Underlying incident (capacity, GPU errors) coincident with config change
- Actions
  - Confirm active/pinned version at the exact scope used by traffic.
  - Check for secondary changes (runtime release, model version changes) around the same time.

2) Mixed worker states after rollback
- Symptoms
  - Some workers report applied_version_id = old, others = target.
- Actions
  - Trigger reconciliation again (idempotent applier should converge).
  - If stuck, do a controlled rolling restart of the affected worker pool.
  - Verify you’re running the build that includes the apply/rollback race fix.

3) RBAC blocks rollback during incident
- Symptoms
  - 403/permission denied from API/CLI.
- Actions
  - Pre-provision break-glass role for on-call.
  - Validate the role in a staging environment (don’t wait for a Sev event).

4) “Version not found” during rollback
- Causes
  - Target version exists in hosted control plane but not in Private
  - Retention / migration issues
- Actions
  - Ensure the version was created/imported into the Private control plane.
  - Keep a catalog of known-good versions per deployment.

Section F — Change management recommendations (Private customers)
Minimum documentation per optimization change
- Scope (deployment/model/region)
- From version → to version
- Rationale (what you’re changing and why)
- Expected impact (latency/cost/quality)
- Canary plan + owner
- Rollback plan (target version, decision threshold)

Suggested canary pattern (Private)
- Create a separate canary scope if your topology supports it:
  - A small worker pool / nodepool
  - A dedicated region if multi-region
  - A dedicated tenant/environment
- Apply config to canary scope only
- Observe for 30–60 minutes under representative load
- Promote by switching active pointer for the main scope

Appendix — Example incident drill (copy/paste checklist)
1) Detect: dashboard shows p95 latency up 35% after config apply
2) Confirm correlation: active OCV changed at T0
3) Decide rollback: threshold crossed, customer impact ongoing
4) Execute rollback: set active pointer back to previous version
5) Verify convergence: workers all applied target OCV
6) Validate recovery: p95/p99 back to baseline; 5xx normal
7) Document: record incident timeline + audit event IDs

Open questions (DRAFT)
- Final key names for Helm values (pending chart release notes).
- Whether all Private distributions will include header surfacing of OCV by default (security/privacy review).
- Standard retention policy for Optimization Config Versions in Private (operator-configurable vs fixed defaults).
